title: Ramanujan Challenge Results: AI-Assisted Evaluation Pipeline for Multi-Format Proofs
authors: Alan Sorani, Ashvni Narayanan, Michael Shalyt, Tali Monderer, Rotem Kalisch, Hila Barkan
abstract: As AI's mathematical capabilities rapidly improve, meaningful benchmarks are shifting from university-level problems and math olympiads to research-level mathematics. The Ramanujan Challenge is a benchmark comprised of research-level problems in number theory, including unpublished results and open conjectures. It presented concrete formulas for mathematical constants whose correctness can be checked numerically, while their proofs may require non-obvious mathematics. Here, we analyze the Challenge submissions, measuring the relative success of different AI models, Computer Algebra Systems (CAS), and formal tools. We find correct submissions that are conceptually distinct from the official solutions, and a proof of one of the published open conjectures. Evaluating the submissions exposed a second challenge: judging complex proofs reliably at scale. We introduce an AI-assisted evaluation pipeline for natural language proofs, CAS code, and Lean formalizations that assesses semantic and logical correctness. Compared with the conventional one-shot LLM judgment, our pipeline reduces false-positive verdicts on natural language proofs from 23% to 6% and improves judgment accuracy on supporting code from 46% to 58%. This approach provides a methodology for evaluating research-level mathematics at scale, with potential applications across mathematics and AI for science.

infographic.key_insight: An AI-assisted evaluation pipeline judges research-level mathematical proofs across multiple formats while reducing false-positive verdicts compared with one-shot LLM judgment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The pipeline offers a methodology for evaluating complex mathematical submissions spanning natural language, computer algebra code, and Lean formalizations.
method: Analyze Ramanujan Challenge submissions on research-level number theory problems.
Assess semantic and logical correctness across natural language proofs, CAS code, and Lean formalizations.
Compare pipeline judgments with conventional one-shot LLM judgments.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports false-positive verdicts on natural language proofs falling from 23% to 6% and supporting-code judgment accuracy rising from 46% to 58%.
infographic.watch_item: Residual evaluation errors remain substantial, and the abstract does not specify sample sizes or generalization beyond this benchmark.
infographic.paper_title: Ramanujan Challenge Results: AI-Assisted Evaluation Pipeline for Multi-Format Proofs

title: An Adaptive Transferable Neural Network for Partial Differential Equations with Anisotropic or Sharp Solutions
authors: Jiacong Qu, Liyong Zhu
abstract: Transferable neural network (TransNet) has demonstrated great potential for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with high accuracy and efficiency. However, it struggles significantly when dealing with PDEs featuring anisotropy or sharp solutions. In this work, we propose an adaptive transferable neural network (A-TransNet), a novel machine learning framework that adaptively expands neurons in regions with large solution gradients to effectively capture complex solution behaviors. Instead of relying on training or random sampling, the location parameters of newly added neurons are determined by integrating the active subspaces method and local gradient analysis based on posterior gradient information. This adaptive strategy enables neurons to be allocated where they are most needed, thereby improving the resolution of anisotropic and sharp features without additional computational costs. Moreover, the shape parameters of new neurons are automatically determined from the neuron density induced by their locations, further enhancing the network representation capability. An iterative neuron expansion strategy is developed, together with rigorous analysis of stability, a posteriori error estimation, and convergence of the proposed A-TransNet method. Extensive numerical experiments on challenging PDE problems with anisotropic and sharp solutions demonstrate that A-TransNet achieves superior accuracy, efficiency, and robustness compared with existing methods.

infographic.key_insight: A-TransNet adaptively adds neurons where solution gradients are large to better resolve anisotropic and sharp PDE solutions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could improve neural PDE solvers for engineering problems with directional structure or localized steep gradients.
method: Use posterior gradient information, active subspaces, and local gradient analysis to place new neurons without training or random sampling.
Set new neurons’ shape parameters automatically from the density induced by their locations.
Iteratively expand the network, supported by stability, a posteriori error, and convergence analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports extensive numerical experiments showing improved accuracy, efficiency, and robustness over existing methods, but provides no quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Assess the reliability and computational overhead of posterior gradient estimation, especially when the initial network poorly resolves sharp features.
infographic.paper_title: An Adaptive Transferable Neural Network for Partial Differential Equations with Anisotropic or Sharp Solutions

title: Researcher-in-the-Loop Evolutionary Discovery of Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Code Families
authors: Jae-Hyun Baek, Byung-Sun Won, Jon-Lark Kim
abstract: LLM-guided program evolution can produce mathematical constructions, but validity, generality, and reproducibility require distinct evidence. We develop a researcher-in-the-loop discovery pipeline that combines program evolution, exact evaluation, mathematical generalization, certified nonexistence checks, and formal proof checking. We apply it to entanglement-assisted quantum error-correcting codes (EAQECCs). Starting from tasks that did not specify a family formula, evolved programs produced finite qubit constructions whose structure researchers generalized to the family $[[n,1,n-1;n-q-1]]_q$ for prime powers $q\ge3$ at $n\ge2q+1$ and for $q=2$ at odd $n\ge5$. Lean checks the algebraic certificate underlying this family. Together with entanglement lifting, the family closes 54 gaps in archived EAQECC tables. The released evidence includes 115 verified code records, ten nonexistence results with checked DRAT proofs, family implementations, and preserved search programs for exact checks and seeded replay. In a controlled cohort of eight paired generation blocks, validation-selected iterative programs achieve success in 46.1% and 31.6% of held-out executions at unseen lengths $n=13,15$, compared with 19.5% and 3.1% for independently generated programs. In this setting, program evolution and researcher analysis turn finite computational discoveries into a proved family with independently checkable evidence.

infographic.key_insight: LLM-guided program evolution and researcher generalization yielded an entanglement-assisted quantum code family [[n,1,n−1;n−q−1]]_q, with its underlying algebraic certificate checked in Lean.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The pipeline shows how AI-generated constructions can become reusable quantum error-correction designs through exact evaluation, mathematical analysis, and independently checkable evidence.
method: Evolve construction programs with LLM guidance and evaluate outputs exactly.
Generalize finite discoveries to prime powers q≥3 with n≥2q+1, and q=2 with odd n≥5.
Check the algebraic certificate in Lean and certify nonexistence results with DRAT proofs.
infographic.evidence_signal: The release includes 115 verified code records and ten DRAT-checked nonexistence results; the family plus entanglement lifting closes 54 archived table gaps, while eight paired generation blocks show held-out success of 46.1%/31.6% versus 19.5%/3.1% at n=13/15.
infographic.watch_item: Researcher analysis remains essential: the reported program-evolution gains cover only two unseen lengths and do not establish broad autonomous discovery performance.
infographic.paper_title: Researcher-in-the-Loop Evolutionary Discovery of Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Code Families

title: Meshless Latent Dynamics Models for Model Order Reduction of time-dependent Partial Differential Equations
authors: Lorenzo Tomada, Federico Pichi, Gianluigi Rozza
abstract: Latent dynamics learning has emerged as a prominent approach for Model Order Reduction (MOR) of time-dependent, parameterized Partial Differential Equations (PDEs). Traditional autoencoder-based approaches are intrinsically tied to fixed spatial discretizations during both training and inference, motivating the development of meshless methodologies. In this context, conditioning provides a natural mechanism for representing temporal evolution through spatially continuous functions, enabling mesh-agnostic Latent Dynamics Models (LDMs). In this work, we introduce a unified mathematical framework for mesh-agnostic LDMs based on conditioning in Neural Fields (NeFs). Leveraging a taxonomy of conditioning mechanisms (weak, strong, and pure), we formulate meshless LDMs as NeFs conditioned on a latent state. We establish a Universal Approximation Theorem (UAT) for this class of models and analyze their stability by deriving Lipschitz bounds for different conditioning mechanisms. Our analysis reveals an expressivity--stability trade-off, providing insight into why more expressive conditioning, despite its higher representational capacity, can potentially degrade performance during temporal extrapolation. Finally, we provide a comprehensive comparison of meshless and mesh-based architectures in the continuous limit of the spatial discretization, showing that meshless models guarantee grid-independent Lipschitz bounds, unlike mesh-based counterparts. Our experiments across Burgers' equation, Navier--Stokes flow past a cylinder, and linear advection show that meshless LDMs can achieve predictive accuracy comparable to or better than their mesh-based counterparts while using only 2% of the trainable parameters and exhibiting nearly constant error across spatial discretizations.

infographic.key_insight: Conditioning neural fields on latent states enables mesh-agnostic PDE dynamics models with grid-independent Lipschitz bounds, while exposing an expressivity–stability trade-off.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These models offer compact reduced-order PDE surrogates that can be evaluated across spatial discretizations without tying inference to a fixed mesh.
method: Represent spatial solutions with neural fields conditioned on evolving latent states.
Unify weak, strong, and pure conditioning within a meshless latent dynamics framework.
Prove universal approximation and derive conditioning-dependent Lipschitz stability bounds.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on Burgers’ equation, cylinder-flow Navier–Stokes, and linear advection report comparable or better accuracy than mesh-based models using only 2% of their trainable parameters, with nearly constant error across spatial discretizations.
infographic.watch_item: More expressive conditioning can weaken stability and potentially degrade temporal extrapolation; grid-independent bounds do not guarantee long-horizon accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Meshless Latent Dynamics Models for Model Order Reduction of time-dependent Partial Differential Equations

title: FARMS: A Verifiable Foundation for Automated Computational Science
authors: Di Wu, Ling Liang, Haizhao Yang
abstract: Automated computational science could accelerate discovery by selecting, adapting and developing numerical methods. This prospect requires mathematical knowledge that AI systems can interpret and reuse with explicit guarantees. Here we present FARMS, a faithful and efficient foundation that transforms computational mathematics into AI-ready computing knowledge. FARMS connects formal statements to source context, algorithmic meaning and quantitative guarantees through source preparation, reusable representations and semantic review. Across 171 targets in randomized numerical linear algebra and numerical partial differential equations, 157 were accepted by the pipeline, with mean estimated costs of US \$0.85-2.29 per target across sources. Lean-checked implications from explicit source premises connect selected statements to computational skills, illustrated by a heat-flow solve and wave-response compression. FARMS therefore supports an affordable, reusable knowledge foundation for trustworthy automated computational science.

infographic.key_insight: FARMS turns computational mathematics into reusable, AI-ready knowledge that links formal statements with source context, algorithms and quantitative guarantees.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a foundation for AI systems to select and reuse numerical methods with explicit mathematical guarantees.
method: Prepare sources and encode mathematical knowledge in reusable representations.
Apply semantic review to connect formal statements with computational meaning.
Use Lean-checked implications from explicit source premises to connect selected statements to computational skills.
infographic.evidence_signal: The pipeline accepted 157 of 171 targets in randomized numerical linear algebra and numerical PDEs, with estimated mean costs of US $0.85–2.29 per target across sources; demonstrations included a heat-flow solve and wave-response compression.
infographic.watch_item: Lean-checked guarantees depend on explicit source premises and cover selected statements, not the correctness of an entire automated scientific workflow.
infographic.paper_title: FARMS: A Verifiable Foundation for Automated Computational Science

title: Experts Exhibit Structured Redundancy: Structure-Preserving Expert Pruning for Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models
authors: Tian Wang, Yongding Tao, Yihong Dong, Xiaoming Wu, Ying Guo, Ge Li
abstract: Sparse MoE mechanism significantly improves the trade-off between model capacity and inference efficiency. However, practical deployment still requires storing all experts, resulting in substantial memory overhead. We show that expert outputs in MoE layers exhibit structured redundancy. Across different models and task categories, the stable rank and entropy effective rank of expert outputs are consistently far below the nominal number of experts, while expert output distributions also exhibit fewer effective modes. Motivated by these observations, we reformulate expert pruning as a structure-preserving expert subset selection problem and efficiently optimize it via a greedy strategy, rather than only independently scoring and ranking individual experts or exhaustively searching over expert combinations. We propose two expert pruning methods under the unified structure-preserving framework: Projection Energy Expert Pruning (PEEP), which preserves the functional subspace by maximizing weighted projection energy, and Distributional Coverage Expert Pruning (DCEP), which preserves the distributional geometry by minimizing weighted coverage error. Both methods incorporate router-derived weights as priors, enabling them to jointly preserve the global structural relationships among experts while accounting for the local importance of individual experts. Experiments on DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B demonstrate that, at the expert retention ratios of 75% and 50%, our methods outperform the state-of-the-art baselines on the majority of benchmarks and consistently achieve the best average performance across both general tasks and mathematical reasoning tasks.

infographic.key_insight: MoE expert outputs exhibit structured redundancy, enabling pruning that preserves shared functional and distributional structure rather than ranking experts independently.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Structure-preserving expert pruning targets the storage overhead of MoE deployment while retaining performance on general and mathematical reasoning tasks.
method: Use greedy expert subset selection with router-derived importance weights.
PEEP maximizes weighted projection energy to preserve the functional subspace.
DCEP minimizes weighted coverage error to preserve distributional geometry.
infographic.evidence_signal: On DeepSeek-V2-Lite and Qwen3-30B-A3B at 75% and 50% expert retention, the methods outperform baselines on most benchmarks and achieve the best average performance across general and mathematical reasoning tasks.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify pruning overhead, deployment memory savings, or inference speedups.
infographic.paper_title: Experts Exhibit Structured Redundancy: Structure-Preserving Expert Pruning for Mixture-of-Experts Large Language Models

title: LLM-Assisted Optimization for Simulation-Based Redesign
authors: Chan-Eui Song, Jeremy J. Michalek, Christopher McComb
abstract: Engineering design frequently involves redesigning a prior solution to adapt to changes in context, such as material prices or system requirements. Redesign often leverages simulators too complex and/or computationally intensive for traditional numerical solvers, which lack engineering knowledge and context, to ensure global solution quality. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret semantic information, including engineering knowledge about the system and changes in context, to help guide search, and recent studies have shown that incorporating this knowledge into optimization can improve search performance. However, how best to combine LLMs with numerical solvers in redesign remains unclear. We develop and test an integrated LLM-optimization approach for redesign and compare three methods for leveraging LLMs (warm start, variable fixing and ReAct) and four black-box solvers (Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, mesh adaptive direct search and random search) on an electric vehicle battery pack cost minimization case study across four types of redesign scenarios. We find that the integrated approach can match feasible design discovery of the numerical-solver baselines with 80% fewer simulator evaluations while tripling the fraction of runs that find near-optimal solutions. We find that the best LLM-solver integration approach and the way the prior solution is leveraged depend on the structure of the design requirement change, and that the benefit of increasing LLM model size grows with the extent to which the LLM controls the search. These results show clear potential for LLMs in redesign tasks for guiding or replacing numerical solvers.

infographic.key_insight: Integrating LLM guidance with numerical optimization can accelerate simulation-based redesign and improve the likelihood of finding near-optimal designs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: LLMs can use engineering context and changed requirements to guide costly simulator-based searches when adapting existing designs.
method: Compare three LLM integration methods: warm start, variable fixing and ReAct.
Pair LLM guidance with Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, mesh adaptive direct search and random search.
Evaluate electric vehicle battery pack cost minimization across four types of redesign scenarios.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the battery pack study, the integrated approach matched baseline feasible-design discovery with 80% fewer simulator evaluations while tripling the fraction of runs finding near-optimal solutions.
infographic.watch_item: The best integration strategy depends on the requirement change, and results from this battery pack case study may not generalize to other engineering systems.
infographic.paper_title: LLM-Assisted Optimization for Simulation-Based Redesign

title: Chance-Constrained Inspection Viewpoint Sequencing for On-Orbit Servicing via Safe Reinforcement Learning
authors: Chloé Carer, Adam Abdin
abstract: Autonomous inspection of a target spacecraft is typically the initial step in on-orbit servicing. Planning close-proximity observation viewpoints involves a complex combinatorial problem constrained by coverage, fuel, and safety considerations. This paper models the viewpoint selection as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP) and applies Proximal Policy Optimization with Lagrangian relaxation to solve it. The system combines a high-level planner, which sequences camera viewpoints on an observation sphere around the target, with a low-level model that assesses each transfer using the Clohessy--Wiltshire (CW) equations for relative motion. The deterministic constraints on single-impulse reachability and $Δv$ cap are enforced directly on the action set. Safety margins are affected by navigation and manoeuvre errors, making the actual clearance stochastic. To address this, a chance constraint on the realised trajectory is implemented, with a Lagrangian multiplier governed by PID control to adapt the penalty during training. The approach is tested on a Galileo-class navigation satellite in medium Earth orbit, modelled as a point cloud where visibility from each viewpoint considers field-of-view and line-of-sight occlusion. Across various risk budgets, the trained policy maintains the keep-out violation rate within the specified limit, achieving coverage close to its maximum and staying within the mission $Δv$ budget. Compared to the usual practice of applying a fixed margin to the keep-out radius and planning deterministically, the chance-constrained policy attains less than half the violation rate at comparable coverage. This makes the collision risk an explicit design parameter, eliminating the need for re-tuning per case. The learned policy selects a viewpoint without the repeated Monte Carlo risk estimates required by a greedy, chance-constrained planner at every decision point.

infographic.key_insight: Chance-constrained reinforcement learning sequences spacecraft inspection viewpoints while treating collision risk as an explicit design budget.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports autonomous on-orbit inspection that balances surface coverage, fuel use, and safety under navigation and manoeuvre errors.
method: Model viewpoint sequencing as a constrained Markov decision process and train with PPO.
Use Clohessy–Wiltshire relative-motion dynamics to evaluate transfers and enforce reachability and Δv limits.
Adapt the stochastic safety penalty with a PID-controlled Lagrangian multiplier.
infographic.evidence_signal: In Galileo-class satellite evaluations, policies stayed within tested risk limits and the mission Δv budget, achieved near-maximum coverage, and produced less than half the violation rate of fixed-margin deterministic planning at comparable coverage.
infographic.watch_item: Reported safety performance depends on the assumed dynamics and error distributions; robustness to model mismatch requires further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Chance-Constrained Inspection Viewpoint Sequencing for On-Orbit Servicing via Safe Reinforcement Learning

title: Improving the Optimization Landscape of Matrix Completion with $ε$-close Surrogates
authors: Ziye Ma
abstract: Non-convex optimization is central to machine learning and AI, yet unlike its convex counterpart, it still lacks a general and principled framework. In this work, we try to highlight the importance of combining noisy perturbations with over-parametrization mathematically under the classic setting of matrix completion (MC). Matrix completion is an important non-convex recovery problem in which only a subset of a matrix's entries is observed, and the remaining entries must be recovered using low-rank constraints. This problem is notoriously difficult because observations are limited. However, we show that by injecting $ε$-level perturbations into the nullspace of the observation mask, we can construct noisy matrix sensing surrogates whose solutions remain $\mathcal{O}(ε)$-close to the ground truth with valid restricted isometry property (RIP) constants. The existence of RIP further enables powerful tensor frameworks to be applied with theoretical guarantees. This approach reflects a broader empirical trend in which stochasticity or noise improves the curvature of the optimization landscape, allowing over-parameterized (a.k.a large) models to better separate signal from noise. Assuming each matrix entry is observed independently, we establish quantitative recovery guarantees without explicit requirements on sampling rate or incoherence, and discuss how such assumptions can further strengthen our results.

infographic.key_insight: Injecting ε-level perturbations into unobserved matrix directions yields matrix-sensing surrogates with valid restricted isometry property (RIP) constants and solutions O(ε)-close to the ground truth.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a theoretical route to improving low-rank recovery by combining controlled noise with over-parameterization.
method: Perturb the nullspace of the observation mask at ε scale.
Construct noisy matrix-sensing surrogates satisfying RIP.
Use RIP to enable theoretically guaranteed tensor frameworks.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical recovery guarantees under independent entry sampling, without explicit sampling-rate or incoherence requirements; no empirical evaluation is described.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish the practical cost or numerical stability of constructing RIP-valid surrogates.
infographic.paper_title: Improving the Optimization Landscape of Matrix Completion with $ε$-close Surrogates

title: H$^2$R: Hierarchical Hint-Based Reward for Mathematical Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning
authors: He Tu, Siye Li, Hongyi Wen
abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards has shown great promise in enhancing mathematical reasoning in large language models. However, existing approaches provide limited intermediate supervision for complex, multi-step reasoning tasks. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{Hierarchical Hint-based Reward}, a framework that leverages the intrinsic sub-question structure of mathematical problems as structured intermediate conditioning signals during RLVR training. Unlike chain-of-thought prompting, these hierarchical hints serve as logically grounded intermediate milestones that effectively reduce the reasoning horizon toward the final answer. To validate this framework, we introduce \textbf{HiMath}, a benchmark of hierarchically structured mathematical problems. Across diverse LLMs, hierarchical hints consistently improve reasoning performance even without task-specific training. When integrated into RL training via H$^2$R, they boost Qwen2.5-Math-7B accuracy on HiMath from 30.4\% to 39.1\% using hierarchical hints, and up to 45.6\% with Oracle Hierarchical Hints. This pronounced improvement demonstrates that incorporating reliable intermediate checkpoints into reward design is essential for sustaining complex mathematical reasoning.

infographic.key_insight: Hierarchical mathematical hints provide intermediate milestones that shorten the reasoning horizon and improve reinforcement learning for multi-step problem solving.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Structured sub-question checkpoints offer a way to strengthen verifiable-reward training beyond final-answer feedback.
method: Use intrinsic sub-question structure to construct logically grounded hierarchical hints.
Condition reasoning on these intermediate milestones rather than relying only on chain-of-thought prompting.
Integrate hierarchical hints into RL training through Hierarchical Hint-Based Reward (H²R).
infographic.evidence_signal: On the introduced HiMath benchmark, H²R raises Qwen2.5-Math-7B accuracy from 30.4% to 39.1% with hierarchical hints and to 45.6% with oracle hierarchical hints.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on reliable intermediate hints; oracle-hint results may overstate gains achievable when hints must be generated automatically.
infographic.paper_title: H$^2$R: Hierarchical Hint-Based Reward for Mathematical Reasoning via Reinforcement Learning

title: Turnpike Properties for Exploratory Stochastic Linear-Quadratic Optimal Control with Indefinite Cost Functionals
authors: Yaohua Hu, Zhaoqing Li, Hanxiao Wang, Jie Xiong
abstract: Continuous-time exploratory stochastic control provides a stochastic control framework for the exploration--exploitation trade-off in reinforcement learning. In this paper, we study the long-time behavior of finite-horizon exploratory stochastic linear-quadratic (LQ) optimal control problems as the time horizon $T\to\infty$, and establish so-called turnpike properties for such problems. In the finite-horizon setting, we derive a feedback representation of the exploratory stochastic LQ problem and analyze its long-time structure. We formulate an exploratory static distribution optimization problem analogous to the classical static optimization problem and identify the corresponding static reference object. We prove a turnpike property for the optimal state process relative to a stochastic reference process, as well as a Wasserstein turnpike property for the optimal control distribution. In addition to the exploratory control formulation, another key feature of our results is that, by introducing a joint coercivity condition, we allow the cost functional to be indefinite and the controlled state system to be merely stabilizable. Consequently, the derived turnpike property is novel even within the classical stochastic LQ control framework.

infographic.key_insight: For long horizons, exploratory stochastic LQ optimal states and control distributions exhibit turnpike behavior around stochastic and distributional reference objects, even with indefinite costs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results provide a theoretical basis for reference-based approximations in long-horizon control that balances exploration and exploitation.
method: Derive a finite-horizon feedback representation for exploratory stochastic LQ control.
Formulate a static distribution optimization problem to identify the reference object.
Use joint coercivity to prove state-process and Wasserstein control-distribution turnpike properties under stabilizability.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports mathematical turnpike proofs as the horizon tends to infinity, but describes no datasets or numerical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Application requires verifying the joint coercivity and stabilizability assumptions; the abstract does not establish practical approximation accuracy at a chosen finite horizon.
infographic.paper_title: Turnpike Properties for Exploratory Stochastic Linear-Quadratic Optimal Control with Indefinite Cost Functionals

title: Exact Theory and Optimal Stepsizes for Stochastic Gradient Descent in Smooth Convex Minimization
authors: Benjamin Grimmer, Qining Shen
abstract: This work considers the design of stepsize schedules for stochastic gradient descent in smooth convex optimization. Throughout, we assume that gradient noise is conditionally zero-mean with bounded variance. Among problems with dimension $d\geq N+1$, we provide an exact worst-case analysis of the expected suboptimality of stochastic gradient descent's final iterate. Our analysis applies to any (potentially nonconstant) schedule of $N$ stepsizes in $[0,1.5]^N$. Here, exact means that we provide a matching objective function and noise distributions where our guarantee is attained. Whenever the variance bound is at least $Ω(1/\sqrt{N})$, our theory provides the minimax optimal stepsize schedule for stochastic gradient descent and proves its uniqueness. These optimal stepsizes monotonically decrease, ruling out any accelerations in expected final suboptimality from fixed fractal schedules observed in the deterministic case.

infographic.key_insight: An exact worst-case theory identifies a unique, monotonically decreasing minimax-optimal SGD stepsize schedule when the noise variance bound is sufficiently large.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results provide principled stepsize guidance for smooth convex stochastic optimization and rule out minimax gains from fixed fractal schedules in the stated regime.
method: Analyze expected final-iterate suboptimality under conditionally zero-mean gradient noise with bounded variance.
Cover any N-step schedule in [0, 1.5]^N for problem dimensions d ≥ N + 1.
Construct matching objectives and noise distributions, then derive the optimal schedule.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports matching worst-case constructions rather than empirical benchmarks, with optimality and uniqueness when the variance bound is at least Ω(1/√N).
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees concern smooth convex problems under specific noise, dimension, and stepsize assumptions; they do not establish performance for nonconvex training.
infographic.paper_title: Exact Theory and Optimal Stepsizes for Stochastic Gradient Descent in Smooth Convex Minimization

title: Neural Network Approximation and Structural Complexity of Semilinear PDEs with Lower Bounds
authors: Hayden Schaeffer
abstract: Neural networks are commonly used to learn the solution operators of PDEs such as the Navier-Stokes equations and viscous conservation laws. On standard benchmarks, moderately sized and often shallow networks achieve small errors that decay at algebraic rates with the network size. These observations are not well described by the current approximation theory, which treats the solution operator as a generic map and derives worst-case bounds over large classes of operators. We show that the structure of the equations and their properties explain the observed behavior. For semilinear parabolic equations, the approximation costs separate into two terms, where one is controlled by an invariant of the governing law and the other by the data. The constitutive law can be parameterized as a single block whose size for accuracy $η$ is $O(η^{-pχ}\logη^{-1})$ for every $p>p_f$, where the structural exponent $p_f$ only depends on the computation graph of $f$. This exponent does not depend on the dimension and is in fact zero for polynomial laws, so for the two-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations the nonlinear block costs only $O(\logη^{-1})$ parameters. The data enters through encoding layers with a bounded number of learned weights per mode, so neither term grows with the grid resolution or the time step. While the analysis only uses the max-norm error of the pointwise block, we show that one obtains approximation bounds in a stronger norm along the whole trajectory. For viscous Hamilton-Jacobi equations with a $C^s$ Hamiltonian, the approximation requires on the order of $η^{-1/s}$ parameters, and we prove a matching lower bound, up to logarithms. This shows that solution operators for this class of problems have low structural complexity, even though they are nonlinear maps between infinite-dimensional spaces.

infographic.key_insight: For semilinear parabolic PDEs, neural approximation costs separate into governing-law complexity and data encoding, helping explain why modest networks can approximate infinite-dimensional solution operators.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Structure-aware architectures can keep parameter costs independent of grid resolution and time step, with only logarithmic nonlinear-block cost for two-dimensional Navier–Stokes.
method: Represent the constitutive law with a neural block whose complexity depends on its computation graph.
Encode data using a bounded number of learned weights per mode.
Derive trajectory-level approximation bounds and near-matching lower bounds for viscous Hamilton–Jacobi equations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical approximation guarantees, including roughly η^(-1/s) parameter scaling for C^s Hamiltonians and a matching lower bound up to logarithms, rather than empirical benchmark results.
infographic.watch_item: Resolution-independent parameter bounds do not imply resolution-independent runtime or guaranteed success when training these architectures.
infographic.paper_title: Neural Network Approximation and Structural Complexity of Semilinear PDEs with Lower Bounds

title: Data-driven Random-feature Approximation of Koopman Generators of Nonlinear Continuous-time Systems
authors: Ana Čukarska, Maximilian Gollwitzer, Viola Muning Li, Vladyslav Fediukov, Zahra Monfared, Felix Dietrich
abstract: Learning continuous-time dynamical systems from data is an active area of research. The Koopman formalism is often used here, because it is a flexible approach that is informative about the system's fundamental properties. The formalism represents dynamical systems through linear operators acting on a suitable function space. A practical difficulty arising in the numerical approximation of Koopman operators is the choice of a ``dictionary'', meaning an effective finite-dimensional representation of the function space. In this paper, we focus on learning dynamical systems in continuous-time, and so we consider numerical approximations of the Koopman generator instead of the Koopman operator. Our main contribution is a data-driven random-feature method to obtain a parsimonious and effective function representation for Galerkin approximation methods such as gEDMD. The representation we construct is data-informed, which allows us to improve upon data-agnostic methods. We empirically demonstrate the suitability of our method for forecasting tasks and system analysis. The numerical experiments show that our approach is accurate, and faster than iterative optimization. Further, we prove convergence of our approximation of the vector field and the resulting trajectories. In addition to the numerical results, we also make theoretical contributions, including a general convergence criterion for the semigroup generated by the gEDMD approximation and a counterexample showing that gEDMD does not generally preserve exponential boundedness. With our contribution, we advance the frontier of efficiently learning continuous-time dynamics from data, towards interpretable and mathematically robust modelling based on the Koopman framework.

infographic.key_insight: Data-informed random features provide a compact function dictionary for learning continuous-time nonlinear dynamics through Koopman generator approximations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports efficient forecasting and system analysis while retaining the interpretable linear-operator structure of the Koopman framework.
method: Construct a data-informed random-feature dictionary.
Approximate the Koopman generator using Galerkin methods such as gEDMD.
Establish convergence of the approximated vector field and resulting trajectories.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments demonstrate accurate forecasting and system analysis, with faster computation than iterative optimization; the abstract gives no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: gEDMD does not generally preserve exponential boundedness, so long-term growth behavior requires separate verification.
infographic.paper_title: Data-driven Random-feature Approximation of Koopman Generators of Nonlinear Continuous-time Systems

title: Deciding two-variable logic with global and local Presburger quantification
authors: Michael Benedikt, Chia-Hsuan Lu, Alex Perry, Tony Tan
abstract: We look at a two-variable logic over finite graphs that allows Presburger quantifiers: linear arithmetic inequalities between the number of elements that satisfy subformulas. The prior literature shows that closing two-variable logic under Presburger quantification leads to undecidability, while closing under \emph{local quantification} -- the counts are always over neighbors of a given node -- preserves decidability. Here we show decidability of satisfiability for an intermediate logic that allows both local counts and global counts, but where the linear constraints do not mix the two. The proof requires a significant extension of the prior machinery developed for two-variable logic with counting. As a corollary we obtain decidability of satisfiability for an important family of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). GNNs are a popular graph learning formalism. For example, in a variation of GNNs considered in the past literature, local aggregation is used in each layer to create modified values at each vertex of a graph, and then global aggregation is used in a final layer to obtain a single numerical value for the graph as a whole. Our logic is motivated by the fact that mixing of local counting and global aggregation in GNNs has been shown to lead to undecidability. Our results here show that if global and local aggregation are separated, one regains decidability. Decidability of other static analysis problems, like equivalence of GNNs, follows from the decidability of satisfiability.

infographic.key_insight: Satisfiability over finite graphs is decidable for two-variable logic with both local and global Presburger counts, provided no linear constraint mixes the two.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result establishes decidability of satisfiability and equivalence for a family of GNNs that separates local aggregation from global aggregation.
method: Allow linear arithmetic constraints on counts of nodes satisfying formulas.
Separate neighbor-based local counts from graph-wide global counts within constraints.
Significantly extend proof machinery for two-variable logic with counting.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a theoretical decidability proof and a GNN corollary, not empirical benchmarks or runtime evaluations.
infographic.watch_item: Decidability does not guarantee practical solver performance, and the result depends on keeping local and global counts separate within linear constraints.
infographic.paper_title: Deciding two-variable logic with global and local Presburger quantification

title: StrictPRMBench: A Replayable Evaluation Benchmark for Auditing Fixed-Score PRM Aggregation
authors: Pengfei Zheng
abstract: Process reward models (PRMs) score reasoning steps, but best-of-N selection also requires a rule that aggregates those scores. We study that rule as a separate evaluation object. StrictPRMBench fixes mathematical reasoning pools, scorer evidence, and the source trace of a deletion intervention, so that different reducers face the same recorded selection problem. Across seven scoring checkpoints and two benchmarks, the stored N=32 outcomes give higher deletion-induced selection instability for product than geometric mean (GM) in all 14 cells. The equal-cell difference is +0.0965; a shared-problem bootstrap, conditional on these checkpoints and frozen pools, gives a 95% interval of [0.0846,0.1086]. A pre-injection-defined sensitivity excludes replacement slots that are either reducer's clean winner and retains 4,459 of 4,622 cell-problem records. The retained difference is +0.0986 [0.0875,0.1098]. Effects are heterogeneous: the two Qwen cells have positive percentile-bootstrap intervals on retained support but two-sided exact paired p-values of 0.0625 and 0.0703. Clean-pool Qwen accuracy does not detect a product advantage, but this is not an equivalence result. We provide versioned outcome records, CPU reanalysis, and an explicit evidence-availability contract. The contribution is a diagnostic evaluation protocol and a reproducible audit of recorded selector behavior, not a new PRM, a universally optimal reducer, or evidence of deployment-wide harm. Raw-score replay and outcome-record reanalysis are distinguished: missing primary edited-score vectors limit independent evaluation of new reducers under the same stress.

infographic.key_insight: With PRM scores fixed, product aggregation showed greater deletion-induced selection instability than geometric mean in all 14 evaluated checkpoint–benchmark cells.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Treat score aggregation as an independently auditable component of best-of-N reasoning selection, rather than attributing selector behavior solely to the PRM.
method: Freeze mathematical reasoning pools, scorer evidence, and deletion-intervention traces.
Compare product and geometric-mean reducers on recorded N=32 selection outcomes.
Reanalyze versioned outcomes with shared-problem bootstrap and a pre-defined sensitivity filter.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across seven checkpoints and two benchmarks, the equal-cell instability difference was +0.0965 (95% bootstrap interval: [0.0846, 0.1086]); filtering retained 4,459 of 4,622 records and yielded +0.0986.
infographic.watch_item: Missing primary edited-score vectors limit independent testing of new reducers; findings are conditional on the evaluated checkpoints and frozen pools, not deployment-wide evidence.
infographic.paper_title: StrictPRMBench: A Replayable Evaluation Benchmark for Auditing Fixed-Score PRM Aggregation

title: Conic-Lifting for Learning-rate-free Convex Optimization
authors: Julien Grand-Clément, Joon Kwon, Francesco Orabona
abstract: A central topic in online and stochastic optimization is to design algorithms that do not require tuning of hyperparameters. Successful strategies in online learning include AdaGrad-style learning rates, Conic Blackwell algorithms, and parameter-free algorithms. However, these classes require different, often difficult, analyses. We develop a unifying family of Online Convex Optimization (OCO) algorithms that require no user-tuned learning rate on convex domains that may be unbounded. The construction lifts the domain to a cone by adding one scalar coordinate, an idea going back to Blackwell (1954). The lifted subgradients are orthogonal to the corresponding lifted decisions, leaving the comparator scale free to optimize in the regret analysis. Applying Follow-the-Regularized-Leader (FTRL) and Online Mirror Descent (OMD) on the cone recovers Conic Blackwell Algorithm (CBA) and Conic Blackwell Algorithm Plus (CBA$^+$) on bounded domains in Hilbert spaces and extends them to finite-dimensional normed spaces with a strongly convex squared norm. For arbitrary nonempty closed convex domains in these spaces, a known gradient bound yields parameter-free regret guarantees. Surprisingly, on an unconstrained Hilbert space, the construction recovers the Krichevsky--Trofimov (KT) coin-betting algorithm exactly. We also give a parameter-free algorithm for unconstrained domains that requires no gradient bound.

infographic.key_insight: Adding one scalar coordinate lifts a convex domain into a cone, unifying several optimization algorithms without a user-tuned learning rate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a principled route to reducing learning-rate tuning in online and stochastic convex optimization, including on unbounded domains.
method: Lift decisions into a cone and construct subgradients orthogonal to the lifted decisions.
Apply Follow-the-Regularized-Leader or Online Mirror Descent, leaving comparator scale free to optimize in the regret analysis.
Recover CBA and CBA+ on bounded domains and exactly recover KT coin betting on unconstrained Hilbert spaces.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical regret guarantees and exact algorithmic recoveries, but no empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Guarantees depend on domain geometry and gradient assumptions; the general closed-convex-domain result requires a known gradient bound, while a separate unconstrained algorithm removes that requirement.
infographic.paper_title: Conic-Lifting for Learning-rate-free Convex Optimization

title: Data-driven Regularization for Inverse Problems
authors: Oleh Melnyk, Sebastian Neumayer
abstract: In many applications, we are interested in studying an object of interest $x$. However, its properties are often not directly measurable. Instead, we only observe $y = F(x)$, where the (known) function $F$ is referred to as the forward mapping. To infer about $x$ from the observation $y$, we seek an (approximate) inverse mapping $x \approx F^{-1}(y)$. This process is known as solving the inverse problem. In practice, the inverse mapping $F^{-1}$ may be ill-defined or discontinuous, which forces us to choose a certain solution from many possible ones based on prior assumptions on $x$. Such assumptions about $x$ are typically incorporated into the inversion process through regularization. Therefore, the first part of this course focuses on the classical regularization theory of inverse problems. In the second part, we transition to algorithmic approaches for solving inverse problems. The foundation for this lies in the variational formulation of inverse problems, where reconstructions are obtained by minimizing specific functionals. Here, we will explore key optimization principles, discuss their practical implementation, and examine how they contribute to robust reconstructions. Today, classical methods are often modified to incorporate data-driven machine learning techniques, which improve the empirical performance. However, this often comes at the cost of explainability or convergence guarantees. Such properties are critical, for example, in medical applications, where one wants to be confident that reconstructed abnormalities are of physical nature and not phantoms resulting from the method. For these reasons, we discuss a number of machine learning methods for inverse problems, such as unrolling techniques, learned regularizers and plug-and-play methods, and explore their performance guarantees.

infographic.key_insight: Regularization stabilizes ill-posed inverse problems, while data-driven methods can improve empirical reconstruction quality but require careful analysis of their guarantees.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable reconstruction from indirect measurements is essential in applications such as medical imaging, where artifacts can be mistaken for physical abnormalities.
method: Introduce classical regularization theory for inverse problems.
Develop variational formulations and practical optimization algorithms.
Examine unrolling, learned regularizers, and plug-and-play methods with attention to performance guarantees.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a course covering theory and algorithms, with no specific datasets, benchmarks, or quantitative evaluation results reported.
infographic.watch_item: Machine-learning enhancements may sacrifice explainability or convergence guarantees and can introduce reconstruction artifacts.
infographic.paper_title: Data-driven Regularization for Inverse Problems

title: Landscape Intervals: A Geometric Framework for Multiparameter Persistence Landscapes
authors: Pan Fang, Washington Mio, Tom Needham
abstract: Classical persistent homology provides a summary of the multiscale topology of a filtration of a space. These summaries are not naturally valued in a vector space, limiting their direct use in standard machine learning pipelines. To address this issue, Bubenik introduced persistence landscapes, vector-valued invariants of persistence modules, which operate by conveniently encoding the behavior of rank functions of modules along the parameter axis. When passing to multiparameter persistent homology, changes in the rank functions vary by different amounts in different directions. In this paper, we introduce the landscape interval, a subset of the parameter space of a multiparameter persistence module which records changes in the rank function in all directions simultaneously. This geometric perspective leads to two novel invariants which serve as notions of persistence landscapes for multiparameter modules. We show that our invariants generalize existing landscape-type invariants: in particular, they recover Bubenik's landscapes in the one-parameter setting and allow us to obtain the multiparameter landscapes introduced by Vipond. For our main theoretical contributions, we establish two exact identities connecting landscapes with erosion distances, prove that our invariants are stable under perturbations, and refine the interleaving-stability bounds for the existing landscape-type invariants. We also show that on a certain class of multiparameter persistence modules, the full invariants can be recovered from finite information about the module. On the practical side, we introduce a robust numerical framework for extracting our invariants from real data and for incorporating them into standard machine learning pipelines. The framework is illustrated on surface mesh and medical image data.

infographic.key_insight: Landscape intervals encode rank-function changes in all parameter directions, yielding two stable multiparameter persistence landscape invariants.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These invariants offer vector-space representations of multiscale topology for use in standard machine learning pipelines.
method: Represent directional rank-function changes geometrically using landscape intervals.
Construct two invariants that recover one-parameter landscapes and yield Vipond’s multiparameter landscapes.
Prove exact identities with erosion distances and stability bounds, and develop numerical extraction methods.
infographic.evidence_signal: The numerical framework is illustrated on surface mesh and medical image data; the abstract reports no quantitative performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Recovery of the full invariants from finite module information is established only for a specified class of modules.
infographic.paper_title: Landscape Intervals: A Geometric Framework for Multiparameter Persistence Landscapes

title: Variance Reduction for Decentralized Stochastic Optimization with Multiple Local Updates
authors: Jie Liu, Nicola Bastianello, Wenying Xu, Daniel W. C. Ho
abstract: Multiple local updates are widely used in decentralized optimization to enhance communication efficiency, often in conjunction with stochastic gradients when exact gradient computation is costly. However, such algorithms generally converge only to a neighborhood of the optimum, whose size depends on the stepsize and the variance of gradient noise. Variance reduction has been incorporated into ADMM-based methods to achieve exact convergence in expectation, but their stepsizes typically scale inversely with both the square root of the network size and the cube of the number of local updates, leading to slow convergence as the network size or the number of local updates increases. In this paper, we propose a novel primal-dual-based decentralized optimization algorithm that integrates variance reduction with multiple local updates, with a stepsize independent of the network size and inversely proportional to the number of local updates (rather than its cube), thereby enabling significantly larger stepsizes and faster convergence. Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, we establish the first linear convergence guarantee in expectation for decentralized optimization with multiple local updates under stochastic gradients in the strongly convex setting. Beyond the theoretical guarantee, the proposed method exchanges only one variable per round, halving the communication cost compared with gradient-tracking-based methods. Numerical experiments further demonstrate its advantages in convergence speed and accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: A variance-reduced primal-dual method supports multiple local updates with a stepsize independent of network size and inversely proportional to the number of local updates, while guaranteeing linear convergence in expectation under strong convexity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method can accelerate decentralized stochastic optimization while exchanging only one variable per round, halving communication cost relative to gradient-tracking-based methods.
method: Combine a decentralized primal-dual algorithm with stochastic variance reduction.
Perform multiple local updates between communication rounds.
Improve allowable stepsize scaling from inverse-cubic to inverse-linear in local update count.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical convergence guarantees and numerical experiments showing faster convergence and improved accuracy, but provides no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The linear convergence guarantee assumes strong convexity and should not be generalized to nonconvex objectives.
infographic.paper_title: Variance Reduction for Decentralized Stochastic Optimization with Multiple Local Updates
